    23                  Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 2026
    24  
    25                  
    26  Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
    27                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States
    28  
    29                  By the President of the United States of America
    30  
    31                  A Proclamation
    32  
    33                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    34                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    35                  amended; Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    36                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended; 
    37                  and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting 
    38                  Imports of Copper Into the United States), I found, 
    39                  under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, 
    40                  as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232), that 
    41                  aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the 
    42                  United States in such quantities or under such 
    43                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
    44                  security of the United States and took action under 
    45                  section 232 to adjust imports of aluminum, steel, and 
    46                  copper articles and their derivative articles 
    47                  (collectively, metal products) so that such imports 
    48                  will not threaten to impair the national security. 
    49                  Specifically, to address the national security threats 
    50                  found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and 
    51                  Proclamation 10962, I established tariff regimes, which 
    52                  included imposing additional ad valorem duties on 
    53                  certain imports of metal products.
    54  
    55                  2. In those actions, I also directed the Secretary of 
    56                  Commerce (Secretary) to establish a process for 
    57                  including additional metal products within the scope of 
    58                  the additional ad valorem duties imposed in 
    59                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
    60                  amended; and Proclamation 10962 and authorized the 
    61                  Secretary to include additional derivative articles 
    62                  within the scope of the duties when the Secretary 
    63                  determined that imports of such products are 
    64                  threatening to impair the national security or 
    65                  otherwise undermining the objectives of the actions 
    66                  taken to address the national security threats found in 
    67                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
    68                  10962. I also instructed the Secretary to monitor the 
    69                  effects of imports of metal products on the national 
    70                  security, to update me on the status of those threats 
    71                  to the national security, and to provide me with 
    72                  recommendations if circumstances indicated the need for 
    73                  further Presidential action under section 232.
    74  
    75                  3. Based on the Secretary's monitoring, I have received 
    76                  information, opinions, and recommendations from the 
    77                  Secretary regarding the tariff regimes imposed in 
    78                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
    79                  amended; and Proclamation 10962 and the national 
    80                  security threats found in those proclamations.
    81  
    82                  4. Among other things, the Secretary has informed me 
    83                  that the additional ad valorem duties on imports of 
    84                  metal products are strengthening the American aluminum, 
    85                  steel, and copper industries and addressing the 
    86                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
    87                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. The 
    88                  operation of the aluminum and steel tariff regimes has 
    89                  also improved because of the actions taken in 
    90                  Proclamation 10895 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), 
    92                  Proclamation 10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    93                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    94                  Proclamation 10947 of June 3, 2025 (Adjusting Imports 
    95                  of Aluminum and Steel Into the United States), which 
    96                  increased the additional ad valorem rate of duty and 
    97                  eliminated loopholes and exemptions in the
    98  
    99  [[Page 18202]]
   100  
   101                  aluminum and steel tariff regimes. For example, under 
   102                  the aluminum and steel tariff regimes, domestic 
   103                  capacity utilization has increased from approximately 
   104                  39 percent in 2017 to approximately 50.4 percent at 
   105                  present for aluminum production and from approximately 
   106                  72.3 percent in 2017 to approximately 77.2 percent at 
   107                  present for steel production, which is closer to the 
   108                  Secretary's recommended objective of achieving a 
   109                  sustained domestic capacity utilization of 80 percent 
   110                  for aluminum and steel production. In the Secretary's 
   111                  opinion, the domestic capacity utilization for aluminum 
   112                  and steel production would not be as high as it is if 
   113                  not for the aluminum and steel tariff regimes imposed 
   114                  under section 232.
   115  
   116                  5. Based on his monitoring of imports of metal 
   117                  products, the Secretary informed me that there are 
   118                  opportunities to continue to improve the operation of 
   119                  the tariff regimes to address more effectively the 
   120                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   121                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. For example, 
   122                  the Secretary recommended that I clarify that ad 
   123                  valorem tariffs apply to the full customs value of 
   124                  metal articles, and he recommended that the tariffs 
   125                  apply to the full customs value of derivative products.
   126  
   127                  6. The Secretary further recommended that I modify the 
   128                  scope of derivative articles that are subject to the 
   129                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704 and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705. In the Secretary's view, certain 
   131                  derivative articles should remain subject to the 
   132                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
   133                  and Proclamation 9705, as amended, to prevent 
   134                  circumvention of the tariffs on aluminum or steel 
   135                  articles or because the derivative article sufficiently 
   136                  contributes to the applicable national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705. By 
   138                  contrast, in the Secretary's view, other derivative 
   139                  articles should no longer be subject to the tariffs 
   140                  imposed under Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 
   141                  because continuing the tariffs does not at this time 
   142                  make a significant contribution to effectively 
   143                  addressing the identified national security threats.
   144  
   145                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   146                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   147                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   148                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   149                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   150                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   151                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   152                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   153                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   154                  amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   155                  Proclamation 10962.
   156  
   157                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   158                  modify the tariffs imposed pursuant to Proclamation 
   159                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   160                  Proclamation 10962 so that they apply to the full 
   161                  customs value of aluminum, steel, and copper articles 
   162                  and their derivatives, regardless of metal content.
   163  
   164                  9. The full-value ad valorem tariffs on aluminum and 
   165                  steel articles, certain copper articles, and certain 
   166                  aluminum and steel derivative articles shall be set at 
   167                  an ad valorem rate of duty of 50 percent, with reduced 
   168                  rates available for certain products from the United 
   169                  Kingdom given the ongoing discussions and for 
   170                  derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   171                  originating from the United States. Full-value tariffs 
   172                  on certain copper articles and certain aluminum and 
   173                  steel derivative articles shall generally be set at an 
   174                  ad valorem rate of duty of 25 percent, with reduced 
   175                  rates available for certain derivative articles from 
   176                  the United Kingdom given the ongoing discussions 
   177                  between the United Kingdom and the United States and 
   178                  for derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   179                  originating from the United States.
   180  
   181                  10. I further determine that it is necessary and 
   182                  appropriate to terminate the aluminum, steel, and 
   183                  copper derivatives inclusions processes established in 
   184                  Proclamation 10895, Proclamation 10896, and 
   185                  Proclamation 10962. I authorize the Secretary and the 
   186                  United States Trade Representative (Trade 
   187                  Representative) to include additional derivative 
   188                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, on a rolling 
   189                  basis, when they jointly determine that imports of 
   190                  those derivative articles threaten to undermine the 
   191                  actions taken to address
   192  
   193  [[Page 18203]]
   194  
   195                  the national security risks identified in Proclamation 
   196                  9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. In 
   197                  determining whether to include additional derivative 
   198                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, the Secretary 
   199                  and the Trade Representative may solicit information, 
   200                  feedback, recommendations, or other relevant materials 
   201                  from domestic producers, industry associations, or 
   202                  other interested parties.
   203  
   204                  11. I also determine that it is necessary and 
   205                  appropriate to modify the scope of derivative articles 
   206                  subject to tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as 
   207                  amended, and Proclamation 9705, as amended. These 
   208                  determinations are based on new information and 
   209                  recommendations provided by the Secretary on whether a 
   210                  derivative article sufficiently contributes to the

    63  
    64                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    65                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    66                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    67                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.)(IEEPA), the 
    68                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.)(NEA), 
    69                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    70                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    71                  Code,
    72  
    73                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    74                  America, find that underlying conditions, including a 
    75                  lack of reciprocity in our bilateral trade 
    76                  relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
    77                  barriers, and U.S. trading partners' economic policies 
    78                  that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as 
    79                  indicated by large and persistent annual U.S. goods 
    80                  trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    81                  threat to the national security and economy of the 
    82                  United States. That threat has its source in whole or 
    83                  substantial part outside the United States in the 
    84                  domestic economic policies of key trading partners and 
    85                  structural imbalances in the global trading system. I 
    86                  hereby declare a national emergency with respect to 
    87                  this threat.
    88  
    89                  On January 20, 2025, I signed the America First Trade 
    90                  Policy Presidential Memorandum directing my 
    91                  Administration to investigate the causes of our 
    92                  country's large and persistent annual trade deficits in 
    93                  goods, including the economic and national security 
    94                  implications and risks resulting from such deficits, 
    95                  and to undertake a review of, and identify, any unfair 
    96                  trade practices by other countries. On February 13, 
    97                  2025, I signed a Presidential Memorandum entitled 
    98                  ``Reciprocal Trade and Tariffs,'' that directed further 
    99                  review of our trading partners' non-reciprocal trading 
   100                  practices, and noted the relationship between non-
   101                  reciprocal practices and the trade deficit. On April 1, 
   102                  2025, I received the final results of those 
   103                  investigations, and I am taking action today based on 
   104                  those results.
   105  
   106                  Large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits 
   107                  have led to the hollowing out of our manufacturing 
   108                  base; inhibited our ability to scale advanced domestic 
   109                  manufacturing capacity; undermined critical supply 
   110                  chains; and rendered our defense-industrial base 
   111                  dependent on foreign adversaries. Large and persistent 
   112                  annual U.S. goods trade deficits are caused in 
   113                  substantial part by a lack of reciprocity in our 
   114                  bilateral trade relationships. This situation is 
   115                  evidenced by disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
   116                  barriers that make it harder for U.S. manufacturers to 
   117                  sell their products in foreign markets. It is also 
   118                  evidenced by the economic policies of key U.S. trading 
   119                  partners insofar as they suppress domestic wages and 
   120                  consumption, and thereby demand for U.S. exports, while 
   121                  artificially increasing the competitiveness of their 
   122                  goods in global markets. These conditions have given 
   123                  rise to the national emergency that this order is 
   124                  intended to abate and resolve.
   125  
   126                  For decades starting in 1934, U.S. trade policy has 
   127                  been organized around the principle of reciprocity. The 
   128                  Congress directed the President to secure reduced 
   129                  reciprocal tariff rates from key trading partners first 
   130                  through bilateral trade agreements and later under the 
   131                  auspices of the global trading system. Between 1934 and 
   132                  1945, the executive branch negotiated and signed 32 
   133                  bilateral reciprocal trade agreements designed to lower 
   134                  tariff rates on a
   135  
   136  [[Page 15042]]
   137  
   138                  reciprocal basis. After 1947 through 1994, 
   139                  participating countries engaged in eight rounds of 
   140                  negotiation, which resulted in the General Agreements 
   141                  on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and seven subsequent tariff 
   142                  reduction rounds.
   143  
   144                  However, despite a commitment to the principle of 
   145                  reciprocity, the trading relationship between the 
   146                  United States and its trading partners has become 
   147                  highly unbalanced, particularly in recent years. The 
   148                  post-war international economic system was based upon 
   149                  three incorrect assumptions: first, that if the United 
   150                  States led the world in liberalizing tariff and non-
   151                  tariff barriers the rest of the world would follow; 
   152                  second, that such liberalization would ultimately 
   153                  result in more economic convergence and increased 
   154                  domestic consumption among U.S. trading partners 
   155                  converging towards the share in the United States; and 
   156                  third, that as a result, the United States would not 
   157                  accrue large and persistent goods trade deficits.
   158  
   159                  This framework set in motion events, agreements, and 
   160                  commitments that did not result in reciprocity or 
   161                  generally increase domestic consumption in foreign 
   162                  economies relative to domestic consumption in the 
   163                  United States. Those events, in turn, created large and 
   164                  persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits as a 
   165                  feature of the global trading system.
   166  
   167                  Put simply, while World Trade Organization (WTO) 
   168                  Members agreed to bind their tariff rates on a most-
   169                  favored-nation (MFN) basis, and thereby provide their 
   170                  best tariff rates to all WTO Members, they did not 
   171                  agree to bind their tariff rates at similarly low 
   172                  levels or to apply tariff rates on a reciprocal basis. 
   173                  Consequently, according to the WTO, the United States 
   174                  has among the lowest simple average MFN tariff rates in 
   175                  the world at 3.3 percent, while many of our key trading 
   176                  partners like Brazil (11.2 percent), China (7.5 
   177                  percent), the European Union (EU) (5 percent), India 
   178                  (17 percent), and Vietnam (9.4 percent) have simple 
   179                  average MFN tariff rates that are significantly higher.

summary.text:
**Clarifying tariff timelines**

I’m checking the relevant executive-order timeline, especially whether the February 24, 2026 change ended the IEEPA-based tariff actions. That would mean no additional IEEPA tariff on Canadian goods after that date, while earlier dates—such as February 10, 2025—could still fall within the period when border-related tariffs were active.

I’m also separating those measures from the independent Section 232 rules. Canadian aluminum may have remained exempt until March 12, 2025, after which a 25% rate or a U.S.-content-based treatment may have applied.

summary.text:
**Calculating tariff outcomes**

I’m applying the stated provisions to each scenario. For the qualifying Canadian cases, I’m comparing 25% of non-U.S. content with the 15% minimum floor: in (a), that produces $35,000, while (b) produces $50,000. If the product fails USMCA qualification in (c), I’m applying the 25% Annex I-C rate to the full $200,000, or $50,000. For (d), I’m checking whether Japan’s listed treatment means the 2.5% MFN rate applies to the full value, which would be $5,000.**Refining tariff calculations**

I’m calculating (d) as a 2.5% MFN duty on $200,000, or $5,000, with an additional 12.5% needed to reach the 15% combined total, producing $25,000 more. For (e), I’m subtracting only the $20,000 in U.S.-produced parts; the U.S.-processed aluminum within the Canadian component does not appear deductible. That leaves $180,000 subject to 25%, or $45,000. The 85% metals exception does not seem satisfied. For (f), I’m checking whether the October 6 entry date changes the applicable rate.

**Evaluating tariff timing**

I’m comparing the stated entry dates with the relevant tariff changes. The 25% rate appears limited to non-U.S. content from Canada or Mexico qualifying under USMCA, while another modification takes effect June 8. That makes October 6 seem unusual: it may test whether a later amendment or transition rule applies, rather than simply the original proclamation. I’m also checking whether the question focuses on the 15% minimum calculation, U.S. metal value, or a subsequent extension affecting Annex I-C treatment.**Checking later changes**

I’m considering whether a notice issued after October 7 could have changed the applicable metal rates by November 14. The stated “today” date matters because the governing treatment may depend on a later proclamation, agency notice, or amendment rather than the original rule. I’m therefore checking the sequence of metal-related actions through November 14, focusing on whether any subsequent measure modified the rates or affected the treatment of the October 6 entry date.

summary.text:
**Reviewing tariff changes**

I’m tracing the timeline for aluminum duties and checking whether the October 6 date reflects a real change or a possible typo. The key milestones appear to be the original 2018 measure, the March 2025 reimposition, the June 2025 increase, and a later 2026 proclamation. I’m also checking the relevant clauses and annexes for Canadian aluminum extrusions, including whether USMCA-qualifying goods receive an exemption or different treatment. I’ll focus on the effective dates and applicable rates rather than treating the unexplained date as authoritative.

summary.text:
**Analyzing tariff timelines**

I’m working through the date-specific tariff timeline, especially the overlap between the two cases and additional duties on Canadian products. The main challenge is determining exactly when each measure took effect, was suspended, or gained an exemption.

I’m checking whether the February action began briefly before being paused until March 4, then whether the March 6 action excluded USMCA-compliant goods starting March 7. I need to verify those dates carefully before assigning duties for each of the fourteen dates.**Verifying tariff treatment**

I’m confirming whether tariffs applied on February 10. If the initial measure was paused until March 4, I’m treating that date as tariff-free unless the underlying text says otherwise.

For later dates, I’m distinguishing the March 4 implementation, the March 7 exemption for USMCA-compliant goods, and the August increase for noncompliant goods. I’m also checking whether Canada was excluded from the reciprocal tariff framework and how separate measures interacted, including later rules on cumulative duties and sector-specific tariffs.

**Evaluating tariff stacking**

I’m sorting out whether duties for aluminum, Section 232, Canada, and fentanyl-related measures can stack. The key issue is whether Section 232 treatment prevents additional IEEPA or reciprocal tariffs under the applicable presidential actions.

For 2025, reciprocal tariffs appear to exclude goods already subject to Section 232, while Canada and Mexico may follow separate rules. I’m also checking whether the 2026 temporary surcharge excludes Section 232-covered products; aluminum extrusions appear likely to fall within that exclusion.**Tracing the duty timeline**

I’m separating the analysis by entry date and tariff program. Even if USMCA applies, Section 232 may still cover the relevant aluminum classification, so the surcharge exclusion likely remains applicable.

For 2025, Canada’s Section 232 treatment appears to change on March 12: entries before then may remain exempt, while entries from March 12 face 25%. A later increase appears effective June 4, making entries before that date 25% and entries afterward 50%. I’m also checking separate exemptions for forced-labor and Canada-specific measures.

**Analyzing applicable duties**

I’m mapping the tariff changes against the entry date and the product’s classification. For the $100,000 Canadian aluminum extrusion, I’m treating the requested amounts as duties added to MFN, not including MFN itself. Section 232 contributes $50,000 under the applicable 50% rate, regardless of USMCA treatment. I’m also checking whether the later 338 measure applies; because the product is in the motor-vehicle-related annex and outside the specified exclusion lists, its September 14 entry may remain subject to the earlier Section 232 treatment rather than an additional duty.**Interpreting September changes**

I’m reassessing whether the September 15 modification makes the vehicle-related duty stack with Section 232. Before September 15, the product’s treatment appears to remain under Section 232 alone. The later language may instead clarify that duties imposed under the vehicle proclamation apply in addition to Section 232 for products still covered by the relevant annex, even when they are not listed in Part A or Part B. Because the product remains in Annex II and has no stated exclusion, the post-September 15 result may be cumulative.

**Interpreting tariff scope**

I’m distinguishing between products whose treatment changed and products that remain subject to existing exemptions. The alcoholic-beverage modification doesn’t expressly add duties on top of Section 232, and the original proclamation excludes articles already covered by Section 232. Dairy appears unchanged, so I’m treating both alcohol and dairy as exempt in the October 1 calculation.

Motor vehicles are different because their treatment was specifically changed, so I’m tentatively assigning the possible 50% duty there. For metal extrusion, I’m reading the later provision as permitting stacked duties despite the absence of a specific Part A or B reference.**Clarifying scope changes**

I’m treating the absence of Part A, Part B, or exclusion-list coverage as important to scope, but not as eliminating the broader stacking rule. For the product in question, the applicable rate appears to be zero on September 10, then 50% on September 16, producing a $100,000 duty on a $200,000 value.

The later provision changes which parts are covered and confirms stacking with Section 232. Because the product remains in the original annex, I’m applying the 50% rate from September 15 onward.

**Determining duty timing**

I’m interpreting the September 15 clause as creating two groups: Part A products become or remain subject to a 50% duty, while Part B products are removed from that treatment. The change applies alongside Section 232, not to products already exempt under it, and earlier entries follow the prior rules.

For product P, which wasn’t in the original Annex II, the 50% duty begins September 15. Therefore, P is not subject on September 14 at 3 p.m., but it is subject at every listed entry time from September 15 onward, including November 3.**Applying scope changes**

I’m treating Q as dutiable through September 14, then excluded from September 15 onward. R remains dutiable through October 29 under Part A, but the October scope change removes it beginning October 30. S is excluded until October 29 and becomes dutiable October 30; P remains dutiable as previously determined.

The October proclamation applies prospectively to goods entered on or after October 30, with no stated retroactive refund provision. For the waiting period, the initial timing appears to run from the July 20 signing to August 22, while later scope changes govern their stated effective dates.

**Calculating duty timing**

I’m identifying the dates for products P and S and comparing them with the statutory waiting-period issue. Product P’s scope proclamation was signed September 8 and became effective September 15, so it took effect seven days later. Product S’s proclamation was signed October 23 and became effective October 30, also seven days later.

I’m also noting the tension with the 30-day requirement tied to the original proclamation and finding. The later scope proclamations characterize themselves as modifications but do not expressly explain how their seven-day effective dates satisfy that waiting period.**Interpreting waiting periods**

I’m distinguishing the original finding from later scope amendments. Product P became dutiable seven days after its scope proclamation, yet the original finding had already occurred more than 30 days earlier; Product S follows the same pattern. The documents expressly describe the 30-day requirement but do not clarify whether adding products triggers a new 30-day period or relies on the original finding. I’m also tracking related timing changes, including the August 22 effective-date adjustment and subsequent product exclusions or scope revisions.

**Calculating tariff effects**

I’m distinguishing the presidential documents by product group and effect: some delay implementation, while others exclude products or expand the covered scope. I’m counting ten relevant documents overall, including three exclusion documents and later modifications.

For the wine entries, I’m applying the suspension’s effective timestamp rather than only its publication date. Entries on August 20 at 2:00 p.m. and August 21 at 11:59 p.m. occur before the August 22 start and incur no duty. An entry at exactly 12:01 a.m. on August 22 is covered, producing a 50% duty on $40,000, or $20,000.**Resolving effective dates**

I’m treating the later proclamation as controlling because it expressly changes the Annex II date from August 19 to August 22, even though earlier clauses still mention August 19. A subsequent confirmation states that the duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. on August 22.

For duties collected before that time, the suspension includes a refund provision. I’m reading it as allowing refunds when implementation requires them, subject to applicable law and standard customs procedures—not as an automatic guarantee. Thus, an August 20 entry should generally qualify for review if duty was collected.

**Clarifying tariff timing**

I’m concluding that no further presidential action was required because the suspension’s expiration operated automatically. The relevant proclamations stated that negotiations had failed and discriminatory measures remained, so the duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. on August 22.

For the 30-day calculation from July 20, I’m counting July 21–31 as 11 days and August 1–19 as 19 days, producing August 19 at 12:01 a.m.; the later suspension shifted operation to August 22.

The annex excluded alcoholic beer, while the broader tariff applied to qualifying goods imported before September 29.**Applying import dates**

I’m distinguishing physical importation from later entry for consumption. Goods A, B, and C arrive before September 29, so the import ban does not apply; however, each remains subject to the 50% duty, producing $15,000 in duty on the stated value. B’s warehouse withdrawal and C’s consumption entry occur later, but that does not change their import status.

D arrives after the ban begins, so its import is prohibited and no lawful consumption entry exists. E entered a foreign-trade zone on September 25, requiring separate treatment under the applicable zone-status rules.

**Analyzing import treatment**

I’m determining how the dates and FTZ admission affect the beer’s treatment. Because it entered the FTZ on September 25, before the September 29 cutoff, it receives privileged foreign status. The later withdrawal for consumption does not trigger the import ban; instead, the goods remain subject to the 50% duty under the second clause, producing $15,000 in duty.

For part (c), I’m applying the court’s invalidation through clause 9(b): the beer returns to the 50% Section 338 duty, while unrelated bans and additional ad valorem duties remain unaffected. Only Annex-listed products are excluded.**Applying duty exclusions**

I’m separating the alcohol, dairy, and motor products by their statutory treatment. The proclamation excludes only the alcoholic beverages specifically listed in its annex and does not broadly alter other Section 338 products.

For the September 10 calculation, Section 232 articles are excluded, so the Section 338 duty is $0. On October 1, alcoholic X and dairy Y remain excluded from the additional duty, also yielding $0. Motor Z appears different: its provision expressly permits the Section 338 duty to apply alongside Section 232, suggesting a $50,000 duty, though the annex scope still needs confirmation.

**Evaluating tariff treatment**

I’m distinguishing the applicable tariff provisions carefully. Heading 9903.82.02 appears expressly covered by the Section 301 exemption in U.S. Note 52(f)(1), so I’m treating both Section 301 and Section 232 rates as zero. The USMCA provision in Note 52(g) was not claimed, but that doesn’t prevent the separate Section 301 exemption from applying.

My current totals are $106,000 under one calculation or $206,000 under the alternative. I’m also checking whether the question requires discussion of temporary northern-border IEEPA duties and the 10% surcharge, including the relevant executive-order citation.

summary.text:
**Calculating tariff timing**

I’m sorting the rates by entry date and checking which exemptions were active at each point. The initial Canada border tariff began March 4, not February 10, so there was no 25% charge on February 10. The USMCA exemption became effective at 12:01 a.m. March 7, meaning qualifying goods entered March 6 still faced 25%, while qualifying goods entered March 10 were exempt.

I’m also checking whether June rates changed and how Section 232 aluminum tariffs interact with IEEPA measures, especially regarding possible stacking or replacement.**Examining tariff interactions**

I’m checking how the April 29 order handles goods already covered by Section 232 tariffs. My working understanding is that it generally prevents stacking those tariffs with the IEEPA measures, but a later amendment may create a specific exception or clarify which provision controls.

I also need to establish when the change became effective, because the answer may differ for entries before and after April 29. The key issue is whether steel and aluminum received separate border-related IEEPA charges or were excluded to avoid duplicative tariffs.

summary.text:
**Clarifying tariff precedence**

I’m sorting out how the executive orders prioritize tariffs on Canadian aluminum. The initial rule appears to prevent Section 232 duties from stacking on articles already covered by the northern-border IEEPA tariff, making the IEEPA duty take precedence. A later amendment reverses that order: articles subject to Section 232 duties are excluded from the additional Canada-related IEEPA tariff. I’m also accounting for the amendment’s effective date and its retroactive treatment of certain entries made after March 4, which may shift the applicable duty from IEEPA to Section 232.**Tracing retroactive application**

I’m mapping the tariff timeline more carefully. The later amendment applies retroactively to covered entries made on or after March 4, with refunds potentially available. From March 12 through June 3, both relevant rates were 25%, so the non-stacking choice does not change the total. Beginning June 4, the 50% Section 232 aluminum rate takes priority, excluding the Canada-related IEEPA charge. I’m also checking whether USMCA treatment distinguishes the “N” and “U” categories at earlier points in the timeline.

**Clarifying tariff treatment**

I’m distinguishing which tariff authority applies rather than treating the rates as cumulative. For non-USMCA goods, the March 4 provision appears to impose the 25% IEEPA duty instead of an additional Section 232 duty, with possible retroactive refund implications for qualifying deposits. The June 4 revision changes the ordering prospectively, applying to entries on or after that date.

Between March 12 and June 3, non-USMCA goods pay 25% under IEEPA, while qualifying USMCA goods avoid IEEPA but may still owe 25% under Section 232. On March 6, both categories remain subject to IEEPA until the USMCA exemption begins.**Comparing tariff dates**

I’m mapping the treatment across the relevant dates. On March 10, qualifying goods are exempt from IEEPA and not yet subject to Section 232, so the additional duty is zero. By June 3, non-USMCA goods carry 25% IEEPA, while qualifying USMCA goods carry 25% Section 232.

After June 10, both categories appear to reach 50% under Section 232. I’m also checking whether later increases or reciprocal tariffs affect aluminum extrusions; because the goods are entirely aluminum, the non-aluminum-content provision appears irrelevant.

**Calculating tariff treatment**

I’m mapping the applicable duties by date and separating overlapping programs. For February 10, 2025, the border measure is paused, the Section 232 exemption remains active, and the later reciprocal, surcharge, and other measures aren’t yet applicable, producing zero additional duty.

For March 6, 2025, the pause has ended, so the 25% IEEPA border duty applies to the northern-origin goods. I’m also checking whether Section 232 overrides or excludes other programs during each period, including any short gap before later exemptions take effect.**Applying March dates**

I’m calculating the two shipment amounts separately. On March 6, both shipments appear subject to the 25% northern-border duty, so each produces $25,000.

By March 10, the USMCA-qualified shipment receives its exemption effective March 7, reducing it to zero, while the other remains subject to 25%. On March 14, the aluminum measure begins, but I’m accounting for later stacking rules and their retroactive effect: the non-USMCA shipment likely remains at 25% under the border measure, while the exempt shipment may face the aluminum duty.

**Calculating tariff treatment**

I’m reviewing how the tariffs apply at each date and separating the USMCA-exempt case from the non-exempt case. On March 14, the non-exempt shipment appears subject to a 25% IEEPA duty, while the USMCA-eligible shipment avoids IEEPA but remains subject to the 25% Section 232 tariff.

By June 3, the non-exempt shipment still faces 25% IEEPA, while the USMCA shipment remains at 25% Section 232. From June 10 onward, Section 232 takes priority, producing a 50% tariff for both. By August 5, the same 50% Section 232 treatment continues despite the higher northern-border rate.**Assessing later surcharges**

I’m treating Section 232 as controlling whenever the goods are covered by its aluminum provisions. The February surcharge does not apply in addition to Section 232, and the IEEPA measure had ended, so the effective rate remains 50%.

For June and July 2026, Section 232 remains 50%. A later Section 301 measure is excluded for these aluminum articles. After the August 22 measure begins, Section 338 likewise does not apply initially because Section 232 goods are excluded. That changes on September 15, so from September 16 the combined rate becomes 50% Section 232 plus 50% Section 338.

**Checking tariff treatment**

I’m mapping the applicable duties across the dates and product categories. The core result appears to be a combined total of 100%, with Section 232, Section 301, and related measures continuing to apply unless an exclusion specifically lists the product.

I’m also distinguishing the Canada and Mexico cases by date: some periods shift between IEEPA and Section 232 treatment, while other periods remain aligned. The potential April 2025 reciprocal duty is another factor, but the non-stacking rule may prevent adding it on top of Section 232 tariffs.**Clarifying Canadian treatment**

I’m narrowing the analysis to aluminum goods from Canada. If the product’s full value is aluminum and it is covered by Section 232, the reciprocal tariff generally should not be added because Section 232 goods are excluded from that measure. The Canada-specific duty may also interact with Section 232 rather than stack on top of it. I’m checking whether any non-aluminum content changes the result, since that portion could face a different treatment. The final response should explain each omitted duty briefly.

**Clarifying tariff exclusions**

I’m organizing the additional duties by effective date and identifying why each one may not be owed. For the northern-border IEEPA measure, the amount may be zero after June 4 because Section 232 stacking rules apply, while USMCA treatment may exempt qualifying products from March 7 onward.

I’m also separating reciprocal tariffs, forced-labor duties, the temporary Section 122 surcharge, and Section 338. Section 338 needs special treatment: it began later, had an exception through September 15, and may apply afterward rather than being categorically excluded.**Calculating aluminum duties**

I’m treating aluminum extrusions under heading 7604 as an Annex I-A article, which means the full 50% Section 232 rate applies regardless of metal content from April 6 onward. Because the product is not in Annex I-C, I’m not applying that separate Canadian treatment. I’m also checking earlier dates carefully: prior arrangements may have delayed Section 232 treatment, while later provisions may affect Section 301 interactions. The remaining issue is confirming the exact Canadian rate for each period.

summary.text:
**Applying the tariff timeline**

I’m distinguishing the rules by entry date and exemption status. The retroactive provision applies the later amendment to entries made on or after March 4, so it can affect the March 14 scenario. For N, the 25% IEEPA duty applies rather than stacking with the Section 232 duty. U is temporarily subject to the 25% IEEPA duty for a March 6 entry because the USMCA exemption begins March 7. By March 10, U qualifies for that exemption.**Reconciling later duties**

I’m applying the nonstacking rule first: when Section 232 and IEEPA could both apply, the IEEPA duty controls until the later rule takes effect on June 4. By June 10, the combined Section 232 rate reaches 50%, while other surcharges, including Section 122, remain excluded when the goods are already covered by Section 232. I’m also distinguishing Canada’s USMCA treatment from N’s ineligibility, while noting that explicit Section 232 exclusions can override ordinary Section 301 treatment.

**Analyzing tariff interactions**

I’m determining whether this product falls under the specified aluminum or steel provisions and how Section 232 tariffs interact with IEEPA duties under the relevant 2025 proclamation. I’m checking the priority rules for dates after June 4, including whether retroactive provisions prevent tariff stacking for Canada. I’m also evaluating possible USMCA treatment and whether the expected Section 232 rate applies from March 12. Finally, I’m comparing the June proposal’s listed rates with the rates ultimately adopted and identifying the stated rationale.

summary.text:
**Comparing rate changes**

I’m comparing proposed and adopted rates across the specified economies. India appears to be the clearest change: its proposal listed 12.5%, but the final measure adopted 10%, after a forced-labor prohibition was instituted following the June proposal. Other countries, including Honduras, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad, may also have moved from 12.5% to 10%, though they fall outside the six economies being analyzed. Cambodia and Guatemala already had 10% treatment. For Switzerland, Japan, the EU, and Taiwan, the framework shifted from flat rates to net-MFN treatment while preserving the same nominal target.**Clarifying country treatment**

I’m separating explicit tariff treatment from assumptions about customs relationships. Liechtenstein was not among the investigated economies, so these documents do not assign it a proposal or adopted rate. Although it has close economic ties with Switzerland, I shouldn’t infer that Liechtenstein-origin goods automatically receive Swiss treatment without an explicit origin rule. The clearer comparisons are Korea, Norway, Switzerland, Germany, Taiwan, and India, where rates shifted from flat proposals to net-MFN treatment or, in India’s case, from 12.5% to 10%. The memorandum’s September 2026 deadline also appears conditional rather than absolute.

**Evaluating timeline and comments**

I’m distinguishing between an expected feasibility date and an operative deadline: the materials indicate feasibility by September 1, 2026, so saying the client “gives until” that date appears incorrect. I’m also separating the initial proposal from the later adopted notice. The June proposal reports over 450 written comments and nearly 60 witnesses, making that claim accurate for the first phase. However, the full process reportedly involved more than 1,600 comments and over 100 witnesses, so the wording becomes misleading if it refers to the entire proceeding.**Clarifying comment counts**

I’m correcting the earlier interpretation: the figures of over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses came from the initial investigation, not the proposed action. After the June 5 proposal, the final notice reported more than 1,600 comments and over 100 witnesses. Therefore, the client alert’s wording is incorrect because it combines statistics from different stages. I’m also checking the tariff changes: seven economies were discussed, but only four moved from 12.5% to 10%; two already had 10% rates, while another was treated separately.

**Clarifying tariff changes**

I’m correcting the statement about seven economies moving to a 10% rate. Five actually moved from 12.5%: Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and Jordan. Jordan’s change resulted from an ART commitment, not a newly adopted ban. Cambodia and Guatemala were already listed at 10% in the proposal. I’m also noting that, after comments linking certain products to forced labor, the USTR removed beef and avocados from the exempt-products list.**Reviewing exemption language**

I’m checking the exact treatment of beef and avocados rather than assuming they were removed. The proposal apparently listed them as potential exemptions, while comments opposed exempting them and raised concerns connected to forced labor. The final notice may therefore mean that USTR declined to grant their exemption and removed them from the final annex. I need to verify the relevant passage before stating this definitively, because “comments opposed” and “USTR removed” describe different stages of the decision.

summary.text:
**Correcting exemption claims**

I’m checking two statements against the adopted specifics. Statement 4 is incorrect: beef and avocados remained on the exempt-products list, despite comments connecting them with forced labor concerns.

Statement 5 also appears too broad. Economies subject to rates calculated against MFN rates may have product exemptions in Annex II, but the negotiated exception applies only to certain listed economies, including Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the EU, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom. Japan and South Korea are not included in that negotiated-specific list.**Refining exemption findings**

I’m confirming that statement 5 is false. Economies using net-of-MFN rates include the European Union, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland, but only the EU, Taiwan, and Switzerland have dedicated Annex II parts. Japan and South Korea do not have separate country-specific sections, and general exemptions should not be described as negotiated lists.

Statement 6 is partly correct: the adopted notice added 471 products in each investigation, including certain sugar and sugar-containing products. However, saying it included all such products is inaccurate.

**Evaluating tariff claims**

I’m checking each statement against the notice’s wording. The claim that no product will face more than a 12.5% total duty is incorrect: that ceiling applies only to certain economies or tariff groups. For other economies, the 12.5% Section 301 rate can be added to the normal MFN duty, so the combined rate may exceed 12.5%.

The FTZ statement is essentially correct, provided it says “once the duties apply” and explains that affected goods generally receive privileged foreign status. If the exemption is invalidated, covered goods would become subject to the duty.**Refining tariff changes**

I’m confirming the remaining claims against the final notice. The severability language supports the statement that, if an exemption is invalidated, the tariff applies to imports previously covered by that exemption.

The Annex A statement is broadly correct: the only reduction involved limiting certain chemical-product exclusions to pharmaceutical applications.

The claim about seven economies moving from 12.5% to 10% because of forced-labor bans needs correction. Five moved from 12.5%; four did so after adopting bans, while one moved for a separate trade-agreement commitment. So the original explanation is only partly accurate.

**Assessing statement accuracy**

I’m distinguishing between what the memorandum’s operative text requires and what appears only in its introductory recitals. The claim about seven economies moving from 12.5 to 10 is substantially wrong: it confuses newly added economies with rate changes and overlooks existing rates and another commitment, so I’m classifying it as incorrect.

For the September 1 statement, I’m marking it partly correct. The date appears in a recital as a projected feasibility point, but the operative provisions do not impose a September 1 deadline.**Comparing document language**

I’m classifying the second Q14 statement as incorrect because it describes proposed-action statistics inaccurately. The June proposal followed an earlier initiative that generated more than 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses; those figures should not be attributed to the proposal itself.

For Q4, I’m confirming the precise Federal Register provisions covering the alcohol and dairy exceptions and the later modification stating that it applies additionally. For Q11, I’m searching broadly for mismatches between summaries, recitals, and operative text, including tariff scope, effective dates, exemptions, and treatment of economies with different commitments.

**Clarifying tariff provisions**

I’m separating the introductory language from the operative provisions, since they don’t always match. The forced-labor memo proposes 10% tariffs for countries including Canada and the EU, while its final language specifies net rates for products from the EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and Switzerland. The related notice accurately reflects those rates. I’m also noting a discrepancy on textile quotas: the preamble mentions possible feasibility by September 1, but the operative text includes no such deadline. Finally, the suspension proclamation changes the effective date to August 22 without revising earlier operative clauses.**Tracking date discrepancies**

I’m identifying a clear inconsistency created by the amendment: it sets the effective date to August 22 and updates the annex, while the unchanged proclamation text still states August 19. The later modification and exclusion documents repeat this problem. Their introductory paragraphs continue describing the duties as effective August 19, even though later operative language correctly gives August 22. I’m treating these repeated references as one grouped discrepancy, while recording each document and page where the conflicting dates appear.

**Clarifying proclamation dates**

I’m grouping the repeated statements by document and page range. Proclamation 11056 establishes an effective date in its first paragraph while also describing a three-day suspension, apparently covering August 19–22. Its first clause changes the Annex II introductory date from August 19 to August 22; the accompanying text confirms this, although I can’t verify the date printed in the image itself.

The original body’s August 19 references remain unchanged. Later proclamations state August 19 for duties, creating a discrepancy with the August 22 start date. Section 338’s timing rule also needs careful explanation.**Assessing waiting periods**

I’m examining whether the repeated 30-day language conflicts with provisions making scope changes effective seven days after signing. The documents may not explicitly state that the 30-day period applies to amendments, so I shouldn’t call this a definitive contradiction.

Instead, I’m treating it as an unresolved interpretive issue: the initial finding may trigger the 30-day requirement, while later modifications operate under an already-active measure. For Q5, I’ll explain that the proclamations don’t clearly resolve this interaction. For Q11, I’ll identify an inconsistency only where operative timing differs directly.

**Evaluating timing tension**

I’m assessing whether the documents contain a genuine inconsistency or merely an arguable timing issue. They recite a 30-day requirement, yet the new or extended duties begin within seven days of the later findings. That appears different from the stated rule, especially where the findings occur on September 8 and the duties begin September 15. Still, the discrepancy may be reconcilable if the 30-day period ran from an earlier July 20 proclamation. I’ll describe this as a potential tension rather than a definitive contradiction.**Checking document consistency**

I’m reviewing whether the documents’ statements align. The suspension dates and the treatment of goods imported before or after September 29 appear consistent. The motor-product scope changes also seem internally coherent: one provision removes products from coverage while another adds them. The trade notice accurately describes the proposal, but the final exemption is narrower than the proposal. I don’t see a contradiction because the broader exemption appears to be the commenters’ requested position, not the final agency determination.

**Comparing exemption scopes**

I’m comparing the proposed Annex I language with the final note f exceptions. The proposal appears broader, potentially covering all Section 232 products, while the final text names particular metals, vehicles, wood, semiconductors, and other specified categories. I’m noticing that some Section 232 goods—such as certain vehicle parts or other article classes—may not be expressly included. The July final notice says USTR exempted products proposed in Annex A, except nonpharmaceutical chemicals, but the adopted note f seems narrower. I need to distinguish the proposal’s scope from the final legal text carefully.**Reconciling the discrepancy**

I’m identifying a possible inconsistency between the USTR statement and the operative note. The statement says all proposed Annex A products were exempted except specified chemicals, while note 52(f)(1)–(7) appears to exempt only enumerated Section 232 categories. Although those categories may cover the currently active measures—metals, vehicles, lumber, semiconductors, and similar goods—the scenario expressly treats the list as exhaustive. Therefore, a product covered by an unlisted Section 232 heading would remain subject to the separate tariff, suggesting the notice’s broad wording conflicts with the implemented text.

**Evaluating exemption language**

I’m comparing the stated exemption promise with the operative annex and the Section 232 product categories. The wording appears broad: it exempts all products proposed in the June 5 notice, except certain non-pharmaceutical chemical applications. However, if the annex omits some products covered by the Section 232 duties, that broad statement may not fully match the final list.

For the related question, the expected answer may be that the only reduction involved certain chemical products, though I’m checking whether the narrowed Section 232 list complicates that conclusion.**Comparing proposed exemptions**

I’m identifying a significant mismatch between the proposal and the adopted text. The proposal described exemptions for certain Section 232 goods, informational materials, donations, and baggage, but the final operative provision appears narrower. It expressly addresses personal-use items in accompanied baggage without clearly preserving broad exemptions for informational materials or donations.

That makes the statement that all proposed exemptions were retained, aside from certain chemical products, potentially inaccurate. I’m treating this as a key discrepancy for the question, especially because the final text may omit several categories described in the proposal.

**Evaluating textual mismatches**

I’m comparing the proposal’s statements with the operative language in the relevant documents. The proposal itself isn’t an action, but its final claim—that all proposed exemptions were retained—appears to mismatch the adopted text, so it may still qualify for review.

The presidential memorandum applies tariffs broadly, with exemptions specified in its annex. I’m not seeing separate, universal exemptions for informational materials or donations. The adopted notice likewise refers only to products covered by Annexes I and II. Finally, the forced-labor notice’s transit definition is limited to goods loaded on vessels and in final transit, with no stated air-shipment exception.**Comparing tariff documents**

I’m checking whether later notices contradict the operative tariff language or merely omit details. The quota provisions align: they encourage imports of U.S. cotton and textile goods and contemplate quotas where feasible, while the final notice’s omission of the memorandum’s three-year duration appears to be silence rather than a contradiction.

I’m also treating the forced-labor-related rate as consistent with the listed economy. Several later proclamations repeat August 19 as the original effective date while recognizing the August 22 suspension, creating a recurring date tension. The 30-day waiting language may likewise conflict superficially with seven-day effectiveness, though its reference point matters.

**Resolving date discrepancies**

I’m identifying a clear inconsistency in the documents. The initial proclamation states that the duties take effect on August 19, while a later amendment says its revised Annex II language is effective August 22.

I’ll avoid interpreting unreadable annex headings or images. For the requested list, I can cite the later proclamations whose recitals repeat that the original duties began August 19 and that the earlier measures lapsed on August 22, including Proclamations 11061, 11062, 11063, 11064, 11065, and 11076.**Pinpointing remaining discrepancies**

I’m narrowing the comparison to two issues. First, the initial proclamations’ operative clauses still specify August 19, while later suspension language refers to August 22 and appears to modify only Annex II. I have the relevant page ranges for the later proclamations and the three original documents.

Second, the July notice’s introductory discussion describes broad exemptions, but its operative footnote excludes informational materials and donations that had appeared among the proposed exemptions. I’ll treat that as a separate discrepancy rather than combining it with the effective-date issue.

**Reconciling proposal changes**

I’m comparing the proposal with the adopted language and noticing several tensions.

First, the claim that all proposed exemptions were retained except chemicals seems inconsistent with the adopted treatment unless the text directly supports that interpretation.

Second, the proposal covered all articles and parts under Section 232, while the adopted note lists only limited categories. That difference needs to be stated clearly, with the final notice’s examples providing context.

Third, the baggage provision became narrower: the final language specifies products for personal use in accompanied baggage, rather than accompaniment generally.

Finally, the notice’s date rule addresses goods loaded before July 24, while the presidential directive focuses on goods entered on or after the effective date.**Assessing transition language**

I’m distinguishing actual conflicts from provisions that merely add detail. The notice’s transition exception may supplement the directive rather than contradict it, since the directive does not expressly address goods in transit.

For proposed informational-materials and donation exemptions, I can’t confidently say the final rule eliminates every possibility because an annex may contain product-specific tariff classifications. A safer conclusion is that the readable operative text provides no broad, categorical exemptions for them. By contrast, accompanied baggage is expressly limited to personal-use products.

**Applying tariff exceptions**

I’m working through each subpart by matching the country or product category to the applicable notes and headings. Thailand and Israel receive the stated 12.5% treatment, with Israel’s calculation based on repair value. For Brazil, the Section 301 duty still applies because the relevant Section 232 heading is not among the listed exceptions. Mexico qualifies for the USMCA exemption under the specified provision. Japan’s passenger car falls within the enumerated exception, so the resulting duty is 0%.**Evaluating Canada scenarios**

I’m distinguishing the two Canadian scenarios before assigning the tariff treatment. In the first scenario, the goods lack a USMCA claim, so I’m not applying the USMCA-based exemption, even though a separate Section 232 exemption may still matter. In the second scenario, the stated claim could activate the relevant USMCA provision under Note 52(g). I’m keeping those pathways separate because the presence or absence of the claim changes which exception can be used.

**Reviewing tariff exemptions**

I’m sorting through the listed tariff provisions and their interaction with USMCA, Section 301, and the newer import restrictions. My reading is that a Canadian or Mexican USMCA exemption does not necessarily remove Section 301 treatment, while MFN treatment may remain duty-free alongside a separate 10% rate. The Section 338 exclusion appears to begin on September 29, so timing matters: goods arriving after an import prohibition may be barred rather than merely dutiable. For the special exemptions, I’m distinguishing text-specific country exclusions from products that are simply absent from the image-based lists.**Calculating country-specific rates**

I’m separating explicit country exemptions from ordinary MFN and additional tariff treatment. Bangladesh and Argentina appear to lack specific exemptions, producing a 10% rate on the stated value. Argan oil is exempt for Taiwan, while Japan and Indonesia require different calculations based on their listed rates. Seed for sowing has an all-country exemption, so I’m applying zero duty there. Psyllium varies by origin: Cambodia is exempt, while Thailand, El Salvador, and Italy require their respective MFN or reduced-rate calculations. I’m also preparing separate MFN and additional-duty amounts for Switzerland.

**Calculating duty totals**

I’m calculating each country’s total by adding the applicable MFN rate, any Section 301 amount, and the additional $4,000 charge. Norway totals $16,500; the UK $14,000; Germany and Taiwan $10,000; Türkiye $16,500; Japan $12,500; Hong Kong, China $16,500; and India $14,000.

Liechtenstein appears to have no additional rate under the explicitly listed action, leaving only the $4,000 MFN amount. I’m treating that narrowly because its relationship with Switzerland could create an origin-classification question.**Reviewing duty calculations**

I’m listing the results for Q6(b): Germany and Taiwan have no residual duty; Japan has $500; South Korea has $2,500; and Switzerland has $12,500. For Q7(c), an $11% Column 1 duty on $20,000 equals $2,200, while Switzerland’s 1.5% Section 301 component equals $300.

For Q7(d), I’m treating the cap as eliminating the additional amount when the threshold is met. Q8 concerns provisional June hearing data. For Q10(f), the cited 2026 termination means the northern-border surcharge is no longer effective by September 2026.

**Assessing duty timing**

I’m determining whether the temporary 10% IEEPA surcharge applies to Canadian goods entered in September. The relevant proclamation imposed it beginning February 24 for 150 days, ending at 12:01 a.m. on July 24, and it did not apply cumulatively with Section 232 duties. Although a later executive order left the surcharge unchanged, its fixed duration means it had already expired before September. I’m organizing the remaining additional duties in a date-based table, using “N/U” values with concise explanations.**Calculating duty amounts**

I’m mapping the applicable 232 and IEEPA duties by entry date. February 10 appears to carry neither duty because the start date was moved to March 4. On March 6, I’m applying the original 25% IEEPA rate to both categories, while March 10 reflects the USMCA exclusion for qualifying goods. For March 14 and June 3, non-USMCA goods carry IEEPA and qualifying goods carry Section 232. From June 10 onward, I’m applying the 50% metal duty, while checking whether that rate changes again in April 2026.

**Calculating applicable duties**

I’m distinguishing the effective dates and checking whether the 50% rate remains in force through 2025 before changing in April 2026. The June 10 threshold appears to be $50,000.

For Section 338, I’m treating August 22 through September 14 as covered by the prior exception, resulting in no additional duty. Beginning September 15, the 50% Section 338 duty appears stackable with the 50% Section 232 duty, producing $50,000 under each provision on a $100,000 value.

The Section 301 category starts July 24, but the aluminum article is expressly excepted, so that duty is $0.**Reviewing Case U**

I’m treating Case U as eligible for a USMCA exemption. I’m also checking whether any temporary reciprocal tariff applies during 2025 or afterward. My current understanding is that Canada does not receive a separate reciprocal rate, so no such additional duty would be owed. I want to verify that interpretation against the relevant provisions before stating it definitively, especially because the timing and interaction of the exemptions could affect the final calculation.

summary.text:
**Analyzing Canadian tariff treatment**

I’m separating the applicable orders and dates. The April order imposed a 10% global baseline but coordinated Canada and Mexico treatment with existing IEEPA measures. If those measures were suspended, USMCA-qualifying Canadian goods would remain tariff-free, while nonqualifying goods could face a 12% rate. Steel and aluminum subject to Section 232 would be excluded from the reciprocal tariff.

For Q15, if Canada’s IEEPA duties ended in February 2026, the later order also terminated the related reciprocal IEEPA duty. I should explain that the duty applied during the interim period, except for excluded products.**Mapping Canada’s tariff periods**

I’m distinguishing border measures, reciprocal tariffs, and Section 232 treatment by date. Before April 5, no reciprocal tariff applied. From April 5 until February 20, qualifying steel and aluminum remained excluded because Section 232 governed those products. Canada’s border tariffs could not be stacked with reciprocal duties; once those measures ended, USMCA goods had no added rate, while nonqualifying goods could face 12%. A later order terminated the IEEPA measures, so no reciprocal duty remained afterward.

**Organizing tariff timelines**

I’m separating each date into two columns: additional duties owed by legal authority and the corresponding amount. I’m also grouping other possible regimes—border IEEPA, reciprocal duties, Section 122, forced-labor measures, Section 338, and surcharges—so their status remains clear.

For February 10, border IEEPA, Section 232, reciprocal, Section 301, Section 338, and the surcharge are all zero or inactive. On March 6, border IEEPA is 25% for non-USMCA goods, while Section 232 is not yet active. By March 14, border IEEPA remains 25%, while Section 232 contributes 25% under the USMCA exclusion structure.**Updating tariff chronology**

I’m incorporating the retroactive March 4 application of the new order and treating the measures as non-stacking. On June 3, I’m recording 25% under the border measure and 25% under Section 232; from June 10 onward, Section 232 rises to 50%, with the border measure excluded.

For August 5, the northern-border measure adds no separate charge because metal articles are covered by the priority rule, and reciprocal duties are likewise excluded. By March 2, 2026, Section 232 remains 50%; earlier border actions have ended, while the temporary surcharge and later Section 301 measure do not add to covered metal articles.

**Clarifying tariff treatment**

I’m distinguishing the applicable regimes by date and exemption. The Section 301 exemption remains, while Section 232 treatment changes: Canada’s aluminum tariff begins March 12, rises from 25% to 50% on June 4, and later applies to the full customs value rather than only metal content. I’m also accounting for non-stacking rules, the March 7 USMCA exemption, and the later termination of IEEPA. For case U, March 6 differs because the USMCA exemption is not yet effective; afterward, the treatment aligns.**Organizing tariff treatment**

I’m confirming that the February 24 surcharge does not stack with Section 232 for this all-metal product, and the separate provision also excludes Section 232 articles. Section 301 remains exempt, while Case U is additionally duty-free under the Canada agreement. For motor vehicles, the initial duty did not stack with Section 232, but the September 15 amendment restores stacking. Because the product is not assigned to Part A or B, later October changes do not remove it from the original list.

**Clarifying operative dates**

I’m organizing the documents by operative date and by the event that triggers each change. The initial measures were published July 23, with duties initially effective August 19 and then amended to August 22. The suspension was published August 24 but operated from August 22, using entry or withdrawal for consumption as the relevant event. Later scope changes applied September 15 and October 30 at 12:01 a.m. Eastern, also keyed to entry or withdrawal. Exclusions applied September 29 at 12:01 a.m. Eastern, keyed to importation, while preserving duties for previously imported goods not yet entered.**Refining operative details**

I’m distinguishing publication, signing, filing, and operative dates so the answer doesn’t conflate them. One document explicitly changes the effective date of additional duties to August 22 for entry or withdrawal; it doesn’t create a separate importation trigger. The September scope proclamation applies from September 15, while the October proclamation, signed October 23 and published October 30, applies from October 30. I’m also tracking which documents impose exclusions or modify product scope, then verifying the requested October filing detail.

**Reviewing filing details**

I’m checking the filing date, publication date, and whether the response accurately reflects the relevant memorandum and trade notice language. The quoted text appears consistent with the notice’s reference to establishing tariff-rate quotas “when feasible,” though the preamble’s September 1 target could create a timing tension. I wouldn’t call it a direct contradiction unless the operative deadline differs. I’m also ensuring the response captures the proposal, adopted provisions, definitions, and Section 301 exemptions, with the existing page citations.**Separating textual layers**

I’m distinguishing recitals and summaries from operative provisions so I don’t treat commenters’ allegations as agency findings. I’m also checking whether tariff rates, product coverage, effective dates, transition rules, and later scope modifications align across the documents. Several apparent discrepancies seem explainable by timing or classification. One possible issue remains: some exclusion recitals say products must already be duty-subject, while the operative clause simply excludes listed products. I’m flagging that wording difference rather than asserting a contradiction.

**Checking duty documentation**

I’m reviewing which products are actually subject to the duty and comparing the annexed lists across the relevant scenarios. I’m also checking whether any later federal corrections or errata changed the documents; so far, I’m finding no such update through November 14.

For item 3, the adopted text adds six economies—Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad—while separately discussing Jordan. The final presidential memorandum lists ten economies directly. For item 5, my net-rate analysis is 10% for the EU and Taiwan, and 12.5% for Japan, Korea, and Switzerland.**Verifying negotiated exemptions**

I’m confirming that Annex II contains dedicated sections for the EU, Switzerland, and Taiwan, but not standalone sections for Japan or South Korea. Therefore, the claim that every economy with a net MFN rate also has a negotiated product-exemption list is false.

I’m also distinguishing the 471 additional products from the separate sugar-related language, so the related statement is only partly accurate. The 10% or 12.5% rates generally apply in addition to MFN duties, meaning a product may face a combined rate. The statements on effective application and severability appear accurate.
